description: This policy brief examines the emerging structure of U.S.–China competition under networked warfare. It argues that competition is becoming functional as well as geographic: the United States and China can shape the same cross-theater conflict environment without acting as opposing belligerents in the same war. The brief distinguishes two forms of functional centrality. The United States operates primarily as an operational-control center, organizing high-end military action through alliances, intelligence, bases, logistics, targeting networks, and cross-theater allocation. China functions increasingly as a systemic-connectivity node, shaping how production, trade, energy, logistics, and diplomatic access adjust to disruption across actors that do not form a coherent bloc. The brief concludes that long-war advantage will depend on the ability to combine high-end operational control with sustainable production, repair, rerouting, recovery, and systemic adaptability.
abstract: U.S.–China strategic competition is commonly framed through the Indo-Pacific or through bilateral comparisons of military platforms, technology, and economic scale. That framing is increasingly incomplete. The Russia–Ukraine war, the U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict, Red Sea instability, Caspian insecurity, and Indo-Pacific deterrence remain distinct, but they increasingly draw on overlapping stocks, tanker and surveillance fleets, transport networks, industrial inputs, energy routes, and political attention. This brief argues that the emerging structure is best understood through two different forms of functional centrality. The United States operates primarily as an operational-control center: it organizes high-end military action through alliances, intelligence, bases, logistics, targeting networks, and cross-theater allocation. China functions increasingly as a systemic-connectivity node: it affects how production, trade, energy, logistics, and diplomatic access adjust to disruption across actors that do not form a coherent bloc. The long-war question is which actor or coalition can more effectively combine both forms of power. The United States must make operational control more sustainable through production, repair, allied capacity, and cross-theater allocation discipline. China must convert systemic connectivity into credible but bounded influence without assuming security obligations it cannot enforce. Middle powers exposed to both systems should reduce concentrated vulnerabilities through diversified suppliers, routes, repair capacity, and clearly defined alignment thresholds.

methodology.framework_name: Operational Control versus Systemic Connectivity Framework
methodology.source_basis: Open-source policy analysis drawing on public reporting, official budget documents, defense-industrial analysis, Chinese industrial data, Reuters reporting, and prior EPINOVA research on continentalized conflict, logistics alternatives, industrial war, network war, and systemic warfare.
methodology.case_context: U.S.–China competition under networked warfare across a wider conflict environment linking the Russia–Ukraine war, U.S.–Israel–Iran conflict, Red Sea instability, Caspian insecurity, and Indo-Pacific deterrence. Analytical cutoff: July 30, 2026.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is how U.S.–China competition changes when regional wars remain politically separate but increasingly draw on overlapping stocks, tanker and surveillance fleets, transport networks, industrial inputs, energy routes, diplomatic access, and political attention.
central_claims: U.S.–China competition under networked warfare is becoming functional as well as geographic.

The United States remains the principal operational-control center, but that architecture creates exposure to inventory pressure, long logistics, alliance divergence, and competing regional commitments.
China is becoming a major systemic-connectivity node rather than an equivalent military command center.
The central competition is between the capacity to organize high-end military action and the capacity to sustain, reroute, repair, and regenerate the wider system under prolonged disruption.
Neither operational control nor systemic connectivity is sufficient by itself.
Long-war advantage will belong to the actor or coalition able to combine high-end action, sustainable scale, repair, replenishment, rerouting, recovery, and political freedom of action.

analytical_lenses.name: Operational-Control Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Evaluates the capacity to organize and sustain military action across theaters through alliances, intelligence, bases, ISR, targeting, logistics, and scarce high-end capability allocation.

analytical_lenses.name: Systemic-Connectivity Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses the capacity to preserve, redirect, and regenerate production, trade, energy, logistics, communications, and diplomatic flows across politically divided but economically interdependent actors.

analytical_lenses.name: Cross-Theater Allocation Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Examines how simultaneous conflicts compete for interceptors, tankers, surveillance assets, transport networks, industrial inputs, energy routes, and political attention.

analytical_lenses.name: Long-War Competition Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses how production, repair, replacement, logistics, recovery, and political endurance alter the value of initial high-end superiority.

analytical_lenses.name: Trajectory Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Defines managed differentiation, competitive stabilization, and adversarial system alignment as three possible strategic trajectories.

analytical_lenses.name: Middle-Power Exposure Analysis
analytical_lenses.description: Examines how actors exposed to both U.S.-linked security networks and China-linked economic networks can reduce concentrated dependence and preserve strategic autonomy.

dimensions.name: Operational Control
dimensions.description: Capacity to organize and sustain military action across theaters through command, access, ISR, targeting, logistics, alliance coordination, and scarce high-end capability allocation.
dimensions.interpretation: Predominant U.S. source of strategic centrality under networked warfare.

dimensions.name: Systemic Connectivity
dimensions.description: Capacity to preserve, redirect, and regenerate relationships and flows across actors that are politically divided but economically interdependent.
dimensions.interpretation: Predominant Chinese source of strategic centrality under networked warfare.

dimensions.name: Flow Centrality
dimensions.description: The degree to which an actor occupies a consequential position in energy, trade, logistics, and critical-product flows.
dimensions.interpretation: Higher flow centrality increases influence over how disruption is absorbed or redirected.

dimensions.name: Route Substitutability
dimensions.description: The capacity to provide or activate alternative transport, transit, or sourcing pathways when existing routes are disrupted.
dimensions.interpretation: Higher route substitutability reduces dependence on a single chokepoint or corridor.

dimensions.name: Supplier Density
dimensions.description: The availability of multiple producers, qualified suppliers, and replaceable components across strategically relevant sectors.
dimensions.interpretation: Supplier density can support adjustment and regeneration under disruption.

dimensions.name: Cross-Alignment Access
dimensions.description: The ability to sustain economic, logistical, and diplomatic relations with actors positioned on different sides of a conflict.
dimensions.interpretation: Cross-alignment access broadens diplomatic and commercial reach but does not imply command authority.

dimensions.name: Adjustment Capacity
dimensions.description: The speed and effectiveness with which production, inventories, and flows can be rerouted, substituted, or reconfigured after disruption.
dimensions.interpretation: Adjustment capacity determines how effectively connectivity can become resilience.

dimensions.name: Enforcement Deficit
dimensions.description: The gap between possessing economic or diplomatic access and being able to translate that access into reliable policy compliance.
dimensions.interpretation: Defines the limit of Chinese systemic leverage when coercive enforcement or direct protection is required.

dimensions.name: Operational Option Compression
dimensions.description: Condition in which an actor can still act, but fewer options remain simultaneously affordable, sustainable, and compatible with commitments elsewhere.
dimensions.interpretation: Defines a major U.S. vulnerability under multi-theater pressure.

key_findings: U.S.–China competition under networked warfare is becoming functional as well as geographic.
The two powers can shape the same wider conflict environment without acting as opposing belligerents in the same war.
The United States remains the principal operational-control center through alliances, intelligence, bases, logistics, targeting, and cross-theater allocation.
The U.S. operational-control architecture creates exposure to inventory pressure, long logistics, alliance divergence, and competing regional commitments.
China is becoming a systemic-connectivity node through industrial depth, energy and trade relationships, logistics alternatives, and diplomatic access.
China’s access is real but does not equal control; economic relations and diplomatic channels do not automatically compel restraint or create security guarantees.
The central competition is not simply U.S. technology versus Chinese manufacturing, but high-end action versus sustained rerouting, repair, replenishment, and system regeneration.
Operational control without replenishment can become brittle; connectivity without protection can remain exposed.

Five long-war tendencies are identified: initial superiority is not durable advantage; flows become more important as stocks decline; defensive success can mean changing exchange ratios; recovery is combat power; and cross-theater opportunity cost can become a strategic weapon.
Three strategic trajectories are identified: managed differentiation, competitive stabilization, and adversarial system alignment.
Current public evidence does not establish adversarial system alignment or an integrated China–Russia–Iran operational mechanism.
Middle powers should pursue diversified dependence rather than passive neutrality or complete self-sufficiency.
policy_recommendations: For the United States, conduct an integrated theater and inventory review across European, Middle Eastern, and Indo-Pacific requirements.

For the United States, preserve crisis communication with China on commercial shipping, dual-use logistics, sanctions enforcement, infrastructure protection, and material support to active belligerents.
For the United States, build a sustainable high–low force architecture and reserve scarce systems for threats and targets that justify replacement costs.
For the United States, expand allied production, repair, inventory coordination, industrial mobilization, enabling infrastructure, and endurance-based deterrence measures.
For China, clarify the limits of Chinese security commitments and distinguish commercial protection, diplomacy, evacuation, maritime coordination, military support, and formal security guarantees.
For China, separate commercial connectivity from belligerent support and reduce the risk that China-linked logistics networks become targets of interdiction or secondary sanctions.
For China, strengthen alternative logistics and recovery networks while improving the conversion of industrial capacity into strategically usable, interoperable, and resilient influence.
For China, reduce maritime and chokepoint exposure while building credible but bounded crisis-mediation capacity.
For middle powers, map dual dependencies and alignment risks across U.S.-linked security networks and China-linked economic networks.

For middle powers, establish emergency procurement and communication mechanisms, diversify suppliers and routes, build selective strategic autonomy through regional cooperation, avoid exclusive dependence on a single strategic network, and invest in recovery capacity.

watchpoints.indicator: Practical coordination on shipping or de-escalation without common enforcement arrangements
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Indicates managed differentiation between U.S. operational control and Chinese systemic connectivity.

watchpoints.indicator: Parallel diplomatic initiatives, competing monitoring proposals, or rival corridor-security arrangements
Sustained Chinese military resupply to a belligerent in direct conflict with U.S. forces
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Would indicate movement toward adversarial system alignment.

watchpoints.indicator: Explicit U.S. linkage of Middle Eastern or European conflict planning to Indo-Pacific coercion
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Would indicate cross-theater escalation of the U.S.–China competition frame.

watchpoints.indicator: Coordinated Russia–China–Iran operational planning or targeting support
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Would materially narrow the threshold toward systemic confrontation.

watchpoints.indicator: Interdiction or attack against China-linked transport nodes on the basis of belligerent support
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Would transform commercial connectivity into a direct target environment.

watchpoints.indicator: Open integration of U.S. and allied allocation plans against a combined Eurasian challenge
watchpoints.analytical_purpose: Would indicate a more consolidated strategic response to an adversarial system alignment scenario.

tables.title: Functional Comparison of Operational Control and Systemic Connectivity
tables.description: Analytical comparison of the predominant form of functional centrality associated with the United States and China in the current networked conflict environment, including primary system role, core instruments, main advantage, main vulnerability, predominant early-conflict effect, and long-war requirement.
tables.source: Author’s analytical synthesis based on Funaiole (2026), Jones and Palmer (2024), McGinn and Dilts (2026), National Bureau of Statistics of China (2026), Reuters (2026a–g), U.S. Department of Defense (2025), and Wu (2026a–d).
tables.note: The comparison does not imply that the United States lacks industrial and commercial connectivity or that China lacks advanced military and operational capabilities. Operational control is used as an analytical concept and does not refer to formal U.S. military OPCON authority.
